results.text:
# Talk about making love before you do it

From here on, when I say making love, I'm talking about two people who care about each other deeply and feel super connected, using their bodies as part of that connection. If you’ve never experienced this, it may be like trying to explain the taste of an orange. If you don’t know what love is, you don’t know. That’s another conversation, and I'd suggest reading my inner child reparenting guide.

Having sex is just the physical act, whether that connection is there or not. But sometimes it can create the connection also.

Most couples don’t talk honestly about sex until they’re already having it, which seems like terrible timing to me. Once we’re naked, saying what I actually want can suddenly feel like interrupting the whole thing or disappointing the person right in front of me.

Before that, I want to know enough about how she experiences sex that neither of us has to pretend. What helps her body relax and open? What just doesn’t work? Is there anything kinky, or anything from her past, that changes what she wants or avoids? I want her to know the same about me. We don’t have to know all of it yet. “I don’t know, but I’m willing to find out honestly with you” is fine.

I’d also rather know what sex means to her. Maybe one of us is mostly feeling bonding while the other is feeling play. Sometimes it may feel sacred; another time it may just be how we come down from a bad day. I don’t need it to mean the same thing every time.

Sex drive is going to move around too. At some point one of us may want more, less, or something different, and I’d rather have already made it normal to say that than discover the mismatch after it has turned into quiet resentment.

Then once we’re actually naked, the question is whether we can still say something true when we think the other person won’t like hearing it. If we can’t, our bodies fitting well won’t fix that.

## Can Casual Sex or a Situationship Actually Be Honest?

Your body doesn’t know that you picked someone up at a bar and agreed it was only for fun. Oxytocin, vasopressin, and the rest can start attaching you anyway. Then the next morning, you’re wondering why they didn’t call. Well, not getting pulled in any further is the best outcome still available, actually, since you just played Russian Roulette with a potential life bond to a stranger.

## Desire is expressed differently for men & women

Women often show wanting directly. They’ll ask for what they want, reach for the man, or even ask him to do something they could have done themselves.

Men tend to make their wanting useful: providing, fixing things, doing heavy work, trying to become indispensable. Not because men are less needy, but their neediness partly consists of being needed. Emotionally, women express their needs more, but this also allows them to get supported more often and by a wider social net. Men, on the other hand, tend to keep their needs to themselves or put them all onto their woman, especially when it comes to the need for a confidant.

If a man is too “needy,” it tends to turn women off. The way women see it, a man should be in control of himself and able to satisfy his own basic needs. After all, how is he supposed to provide for somebody else if he can't manage himself?

It's not that male pursuit is a turn-off to women (assuming they are interested in the man), but they want to see that the man can pursue strongly while staying grounded. The polarity evaporates when he keeps reaching without satisfaction, loses control of himself, or makes the woman responsible for regulating his emotions.

## Not A Performance

I don’t actually think of myself as especially masculine. I step into that energy when I see that a woman would appreciate it, and then it comes naturally. If I have to keep proving I’m “the man,” I start defending the role every time I hesitate, cry, need help, or get something wrong.

Bee once called me her “wife.” I don’t recommend that as a polarity exercise, by the way.

I don’t need her acting soft, helpless, or cute every minute to prove anything either. Surrender means more to me when I know she could take control and just doesn’t want to right then.

“Honey, how do you see this intuitively?”

or, “Can you help me think through the practical side for a minute?”

results.text:
# What are you actually choosing together?

A lot of romantic pain starts with two lovey bunnies entering one of the biggest arrangements of their lives without ever discussing their ideas, dreams, and fears about it.

“We’re together” can hide a lot. I might hear exclusivity, living together, shared money, children, caregiving, and a whole future, while she hears, “We really like each other and we’ll see.” I don’t mind letting some things develop without naming them. I mind finding out later that one of us thought the label had already settled them.

Maybe what two people actually want is mostly practical: share a home, raise children, support each other, take care of each other, and maybe have sex. That’s common, especially outside the modern West. If both people know what they’re doing, I don’t think there’s anything inherently wrong with it. It would feel wrong to me because I want to be in love. I’d also be thinking about what happens if one of us later meets somebody we really do fall for and starts wondering why we settled.

What I want is romance without pretending I can promise a future emotion. Two people can really be in love and choose exclusivity, shack up, have children, and plan a life together. I still can’t know exactly what my heart will feel ten years from now.

So before I commit, I want to know what we think we’re actually joining and what we’re really promising. If the romance changes, which parts are supposed to remain? What happens if one of us falls in love with someone else? Is that itself betrayal, or does betrayal mean lying or breaking an agreement? Which needs are we expecting to keep outside the relationship? When do we revisit the agreement? If we separate, what do we still owe each other and any children?

My actual ideal is still to have intimacy embedded in community. Most people aren’t going to move into a free-love community, so as Pema Chödrön says, “Start Where You Are.” Keep friendships and other sources of meaning and support alive while you figure out what kind of relationship you’re actually building.
